Formal verification using Hoare logic is widely employed for precisely defining software behaviors, yet translating specifications into the required three-part format can be challenging. SoftSpec addresses this issue by utilizing natural language to represent requirements, integrating a deferrable predicate within it for later interpretation. To facilitate this, we introduce a new formal framework called n-formula, which mirrors common logical phrases found in everyday language. When paired with a natural language specification, n-formula enables the partitioning of software requirements, leading to fully verified programs, as demonstrated through our analysis of the Apache Commons Lang library in relation to natural language requirements.

Distributed consensus is a foundational concept for reliable operation in distributed systems.  All systems, however, are susceptible to failures.  In best-case scenarios, these failures are of a basic nature -- the system may lose connection to some nodes, after which the consensus protocol must initiate a new round.  More complex situations arise when nodes can also send incorrect data to the network, necessitating a more robust approach.  Canopus is a distributed consensus protocol designed to handle the most complex failure scenarios, yet it is limited in that it can only address this issue once a failure is detected.  Recognizing that Canopus's vulnerability to unexpected failures poses a significant challenge, RCanopus is introduced as a novel resilience layer that both detects failures and integrates with Canopus to ensure that the system can continue forward with confidence in the face of failures.  By providing an interface for detecting failures, ensuring that only one copy of the new key is active, and adapting Canopus to include re-keying functionality, RCanopus offers a level of reliability that far exceeds the existing capabilities of consensus protocols.  Furthermore, we present Yellows, a concrete implementation of RCanopus, built upon Canopus and supported by the Google Kubernetes Engine.

Using an advanced molecular dynamics simulation, we investigated how to accurately measure lipid behavior by testing it on a diverse range of cholesterol-containing lipid types. We discovered that existing evaluation methods can yield significantly different results, highlighting the necessity of employing multiple estimation techniques. We analyzed the influence of testing setup variations, such as testing duration, on estimated material properties, and found that some estimation methods are more reliable for specific testing configurations. Our findings reveal that including cholesterol in a lipid type generally increases its resistance to bending but has little to no impact on its surface tension or lateral movement within the testing environment.

This paper examines the loop quantum cosmological model generated from the ADM Hamiltonian. Following the procedure used in ref. [1], but applying it to the full 3+1 ADM 1-loop model as opposed to the 3-1 Hoyle LQC model, we derive the Schrödinger equation governing particle motion in this model. This derivation confirms that the particle behaves as if moving through an elastic medium characterized by a potential derived from the difference between the Lorentzian kernel's bounce point and Fermi's $k_{FIRP}$ 's bounce point in the full 3+1 ADM LQC model. This outcome aligns with the predictions made in the Hojleski-Tulczyjew ADM model.

The Pierre Auger Observatory catalog details 100 extensive air showers
observed during the initial phase of its Central Detector's operation, featuring
extreme energy levels. With an estimated uncertainty of 16%, these events possess
the greatest energy of any cosmic particles ever detected, surpassing $10^{20}$ eV.
Characterized by a 16° angular separation, this catalog represents an enriched subset
of 417 events recorded over 12 years of observations, each exhibiting maximum energy
uncertainty of 15%. Statistically, this catalog catalog showcases an apparent overabundance
of ultra-high-energy cosmic rays at the highest recorded energies.

Accurate uncertainty estimation is a critical component of deep object detectors, enabling the evaluation of detection accuracy and error rates in various environments. It facilitates informed decision-making in complex situations, such as detecting anomalies, reducing false alarms, and making informed choices about when to trust detection results. Current methods for estimating uncertainty fall into two main categories: likelihood-based and empirical likelihood-based approaches. However, these methods have limitations, primarily requiring a predefined detection model, which limits their adaptability and applicability in various real-world scenarios. This paper presents a novel Bayesian approach to uncertainty estimation, referred to as BayesOD, designed to work with existing object detectors without requiring any additional training. BayesOD leverages the probabilistic nature of uncertainty estimation to overcome the limitations of traditional methods and provides reliable uncertainty estimates in diverse detection models. Extensive evaluations demonstrate that BayesOD outperforms existing probabilistic and empirical likelihood-based approaches, showcasing its versatility and robustness in various object detection models and architectures.

The effectiveness of future traffic forecasting is heavily influenced by the accuracy of short-term traffic pattern predictions.
To address this, a new framework called Traffic Moving Snippets (TMS) is proposed, which focuses on accurately predicting transient traffic patterns over a large area.
Unlike traditional pixel-based methods, TMS is based on a dictionary of dynamic traffic patterns and uses an iterative optimization technique to represent complex image content.
This framework is capable of handling diverse traffic characteristics, including variations in lighting, camera angles, and geographical locations.
By integrating the content from the best-matching snippet dictionary elements, TMS is able to generate high-quality traffic forecasts over a wide area.
Experiments conducted on public datasets demonstrate the superiority of the proposed framework in terms of accuracy and efficiency.

In recent years, rewriting theory has been applied to solve problems in category theory, mirroring its success in programming. We've extended rewriting theory to address the challenge of rewriting $\mathcal{G}$-morphisms, where $\mathcal{G}$ is a Gray category. This has led to a framework for selecting congruent reductions applicable to arbitrary rewrite systems. Our framework has been used to demonstrate that any rewrite system with a finite codomain possesses a set of complete morphisms, a concept that has potential applications in the theory of finitely generated monoids, finite-dimensional vector spaces, and finite CW complexes.

Automatic hippocampus segmentation in neurodegenerative disease research and epilepsy is a crucial task that has been made difficult by studies with limited data volumes and varied imaging protocols. This work proposes and evaluates an ensemble of three convolutional neural networks designed for hippocampus segmentation, which demonstrates superior performance compared to a single network. By training and testing these networks individually on a consistent subset of cases, the results indicate that the ensemble achieves enhanced accuracy, robustness, and invariance, without compromising computational efficiency. A novel ensemble arrangement is also introduced, which trains networks on overlapping case subsets, thereby reducing memory usage while maintaining high performance.

A long-standing phenomenon in quantum optics, first observed by Piret and Piron in 1987, reveals that two-photon states of the same polarization are less likely to interact when passing through perpendicular detectors compared to single-photon states. Over the past 45 years, numerous experiments have confirmed this effect, yet a theoretical explanation remained elusive until now. In this research, we revisit the phenomenon using a more complex mode structure, incorporating both spatial and polarization modes, and demonstrate that the apparent suppression of interference is an illusion resulting from the phenomenon's inherent dependence on mode selection. By expanding two-photon states into different mode bases, we show that the perceived suppression merely reflects the absence of overlap between these states and the chosen detection modes, thereby resolving the puzzle for over four decades.

Previous research indicates that trapped cosmic ray particles can generate significant ionization, 
limiting the use of electromagnetic communications within Earth's orbit. 
To better understand this effect, a new approach is taken to simulate 
cosmic ray particles' behavior by calculating their low Earth orbit 
ionization using a Monte Carlo method. 
This involves determining the particles' density and energy distribution 
at various points using a specialized equation, and then applying a 
low Earth orbit correction based on additional magnetic field data. 
The results show that the particles' behavior can significantly impact 
ionization levels and that the established cosmic ray ambient geomagnetic 
model is not sufficient for accurate simulations. 
To refine the simulations, a new cosmic ray low Earth orbit ambient 
geomagnetic model is applied, and the simulations are validated using 
real-time measurements.

A network's expressivity and generalization capabilities are essential to assess the effectiveness of Deep Graph Neural Networks (GNNs). This study proposes an innovative pyramidal Deep Graph Shrinkage Skeleton (PDSK) framework, which globaly condenses the input graph's skeleton by leveraging its inherent topological features. By doing so, it provides guidance on GNN architecture design, making it more interpretable and reliable. Furthermore, a local Pyramidal Deep Graph Rewiring (PYDR) module is introduced to refine GNN architecture details, demonstrating that GNN performance can be enhanced by both global and local graph shrinks. Evaluations across eight benchmark tasks, including node classification, link prediction, and graph classification, validate PDSK's effectiveness.

This work presents a private method for low-rank matrix completion, where we show that adding noise based on the Huber norm yields a differentially private algorithm. Our analysis reveals the first bound on the mean square error of the noise, which approaches the limit of noise minimization as the number of queries tends to infinity. Furthermore, we challenge the assumption that private low-rank matrix completion with known matrix nuclear norm is already effectively achieving minimal noise, by providing evidence to the contrary. We also situate our research within the context of private spectral clustering, where we introduce a novel clustering algorithm that achieves privacy through noise addition.

We introduce The Astrodust + PAH model, an advanced approach to understanding the optical and near-infrared behavior of interstellar dust. This model integrates a detailed, microscopic description of dust particles with a broader approach to model larger dust grains. As a result, our model accurately predicts the behavior of interstellar dust across a wide range of wavelengths, from optical to far-infrared, and adequately explains observed phenomena like polarization and emission characteristics. Notably, our model successfully predicts the extreme levels of dust polarization observed in the far-infrared, and accurately explains the observed PAH polarization fraction trends. Furthermore, our model demonstrates that the polarization fraction decreases as wavelengths increase, and inversely correlates with extinction levels. Additionally, our model suggests that the observed PAH polarization increases when observed through aligned dust grains. Lastly, our model accurately explains the observed ratios of extinction to emission, and accurately predicts the observed near-infrared slope values.

The formation of low mass stars and their surrounding disks is significantly influenced by massive planets.  Observations of disk structure in these systems can provide crucial insights into the presence of these planets.  CIDA 1, a low mass star in the Cetus star forming region, has two protoplanetary disks that are heavily inclined to each other.  To understand the physical properties of these disks, we analyzed the mid-infrared emissions from CIDA 1, using the Spitzer Space Telescope.  Our findings revealed that the dust in the disks is being shaped by a massive planet, with a mass of 10 Jupiter masses, orbiting at a distance of 10-20 astronomical units.  This discovery provides further evidence that external forces, such as massive planets, play a crucial role in the formation and shaping of protoplanetary disks.

Consider a simple graph, G, that undergoes the Lights Out process, starting with all vertices in the 'on' state. When a vertex is clicked, it toggles its own state and the states of its adjacent vertices. Research has shown certain properties regarding the number of required clicks to turn all vertices 'off', specifically a maximum of n-1 clicks for n vertices, which is exactly n when G is connected. This paper investigates specific structural characteristics of graphs to determine if they achieve the minimum number of clicks, focusing particularly on bipartite graphs where the maximum number of required clicks is achieved.

This paper presents a novel, multi-stage image segmentation model, designed to overcome the challenges posed by degraded variational image segmentation methods when processing low-quality images. To tackle this issue, we break down the segmentation process into two stages: a low-quality to high-quality image transformation and a surface segmentation of the restored image. To achieve this, we employ two level set-based variational models, one for restoring the image and another for segmenting the restored image. To enhance robustness to low-quality images with severe noise or corruption, our image restoration model incorporates a new optimization term combining the characteristics of total variation and deep learning-driven synthesis. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our proposed model achieves superior image quality and precise segmentation compared to current state-of-the-art methods.

Program analysis through Abstract Interpretation involves simulating the behavior of a program in a simplified environment to approximate its true behavior. This simulation typically has two parts: the forward phase calculates an approximation of a program's state as it moves through its structure, while the backward phase uses a technique called widening to ensure the process converges within a reasonable time. However, this traditional approach can cause a delay as widening only comes into play between phases. A new efficient backward phase with adjusted convergence is presented, reducing widening in the forward phase and improving overall performance. This innovation, based on a novel mathematical concept, overcomes the limitations of traditional methods and offers simplified implementations.

Our research demonstrates a fresh optical strategy for manipulating topological phonons within oxide perovskites that can enable efficient conversion of light to mechanical energy and enhance quantum sound communications. By utilizing the strong light-matter connection in these materials, we can use laser pulses to not only create specific mechanical sound patterns, but also convert them into a complex form of mechanical sound called a topological phonon. By adjusting the intensity of the laser pulse, we can convert two-dimensional mechanical sound into a three-dimensional topological phonon state, thereby achieving efficient light-mechanical energy conversion and enhancing quantum sound communications.

Unsupervised outlier detection in various fields such as data mining and machine learning relies heavily on distance-based techniques, despite their high computational costs. Traditional methods typically involve repeated nearest neighbor searches. This paper presents an innovative approach, combining the strength of the Partially and Iteratively Constructed Graph (PIRG) with distance-based density separation measures, providing an exact solution. The proposed method offers improved performance over the widely used k-Nearest Neighbors (k-NN) method, with experiments showing significant speedups for high-dimensional data. Furthermore, this solution enables the adaptation of density separation measures without expensive nearest neighbor searches.

An atom exhibiting multiple energy levels remains stationary near a thin, perfectly reflective ideal mirror until a second ideal moving mirror is introduced at right angles to the first. Due to its motion, the secondary mirror excites certain energy transitions within the atom, and as a result, it emits electromagnetic radiation corresponding to those excited states. Using quantum electrodynamics theory, we calculate the probability of this excitation and determine the energy emitted as electromagnetic radiation for various scenarios, including those involving imperfect mirrors. We also provide additional context by discussing a similar scenario in which an atom remains stationary between two parallel, ideal reflective mirrors, one of which is in motion. Under specific conditions, the motion of the secondary mirror causes the atom to become excited, leading to electromagnetic radiation emission. Moreover, we find that excited energy states within the atom may experience additional acceleration as a result of this phenomenon.

When training a graph representation learning model, it's crucial to consider fairness, especially 3rd party data availability. To address this, we propose an approach that uses fairness constraints based on neighborhood fairness, taking into account sensitive attributes. By converting sensitivity labels into graph form, we can more effectively enforce fairness constraints during model training. A key challenge arises when a subset of labels has no connections to other nodes, but we can still estimate the neighborhood fairness by modeling it as a Markov chain. Experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach, outperforming a baseline in achieving 5% higher accuracy while maintaining comparable AUC values, and showing 95.2% AUC performance with only 94.8% AUC for neighborhood fairness constraint.

This research focuses on kinetic models for reversible enzyme reactions and evaluates the effectiveness of two analytical techniques in obtaining approximate solutions to these models. We apply the homotopy analysis method and the homotopy analysis scheme method to derive these solutions, using the latter in combination with the least squares approach to determine unknown coefficients. Although both techniques yield similar results, our study demonstrates that the homotopy analysis scheme method may be more suitable than the homotopy analysis method for certain applications.

Theoretical predictions for natural supersymmetry, a theory where the Higgs mass is naturally close to its current value, are being tested through particle collisions at a high-energy accelerator.  Researchers are analyzing data collected from these collisions at 13 TeV, where two high-energy particles collide and produce additional energy that is not visible to detectors.  Using a dataset of 35.9 inverse femtobarns, they searched for signs of supersymmetry by examining various patterns of energy and momentum.  They focused on scenarios involving simple supersymmetric models and more complex supersymmetric theories, using different types of initial particles and decay patterns.  In particular, they looked at scenarios involving the Higgs-like particle and various supersymmetric particles, including a light neutralino, which is a potential dark matter candidate.  By comparing the observed data to predictions based on the standard model of particle physics, they found no signs of supersymmetry.  As a result, they set limits on scenarios involving simple supersymmetric models and more complex supersymmetric theories, excluding various combinations of particle masses and production rates at different energy levels.  These findings further constrain theories of natural supersymmetry, further limiting the parameter space available for these scenarios.

We introduce a new rational expectations model, specifically for financial bubbles, and provide mathematical tools to identify the key parameters that define both the model's behavior and its return to normality. Our stochastic model features a key variable that controls the model's return to normality, which has a stable average value and fluctuates in a predictable manner. Through thorough mathematical analysis, we show that our model can exhibit the complex patterns seen in real markets. We also present a mathematical proof of the model's existence and uniqueness, which ensures the model's stability. We utilize the VSS algorithm to find the complex values associated with our model, which guarantees its stability. We provide a clear criterion for adjusting the model's key variable to ensure the model's return to normality. We utilize high-frequency data from cryptocurrency markets, specifically for Ravencoin, to diagnose the model's key parameters. Our analysis demonstrates that adjusting the model's key variable can effectively control the model's behavior, which we show through statistical tests of our model's predictions against the actual market returns.

Quantum harmonic oscillators were computationally investigated with the help of statistical mechanics path integral simulations. By employing Monte Carlo sampling techniques, researchers were able to obtain numerical solutions for these systems at finite temperatures. In systems with time-dependent interactions, the simulation approach was found to be dependent on initial conditions and yielded solutions in the form of real trajectories, which were found to exhibit excellent agreement with analytical predictions derived from the Schrödinger equation.

Recent research has shown that combining item-user interactions and sentiment analysis with deep learning methods is an effective approach for analyzing online product reviews. However, current systems primarily focus on either the review text or user interactions with items separately. To bridge this gap, a new method called Sentiment-aware Interactive Fusion (SIFN) is proposed, blending sentiment analysis with interactive feature mining to create a comprehensive, item-representation that considers both aspects. By leveraging sentiment-aware elements to fuse these features, SIFN can effectively blend review-based text features with user-item interaction features, ultimately leading to more accurate and diverse recommendations. Experimental results on two large datasets demonstrate that SIFN outperforms existing recommendation methods by providing more precise online suggestions.

This study investigates dialectal Arabic to Standard Arabic translations for data augmentation in Arabic-English machine translation. Creating parallel dialectal Arabic and Standard Arabic texts is crucial for developing effective machine translators. We examine three dialects (Egyptian, Gulf, and Israeli) in detail, and the results show that these analyses could potentially contribute to developing more capable dialectal Arabic Arabic-English MT systems.

We show that any subgroup of homeomorphisms of a compact surface that fix the boundary, whose action within the surface's interior is highly transitive, cannot be topologically compact when using the compact-open topology's induced subtopology.

We're investigating integrable boundary conditions that can be geometrically interpreted as D-branes within specific theoretical models based on products of group-like models and cosets, which generalize the lambda deformation. Through this approach, we're able to establish a relationship with undeformed coset models, where previously known branes can be accurately recreated. Additionally, we're deriving novel branes that were previously undiscovered, which exhibit intriguing properties, such as being spatially extended across the entire worldsheet or confined to specific points, and others with worldsheet conformal properties that fluctuate between these two extremes.

Tetrahedral meshes play a pivotal role in solving partial differential equations and are extensively used in computer graphics and biology.  A key challenge lies in effectively converting these meshes into lower polyhedra for shape-mapping applications.  To address this, we propose the use of a Tets/Hex class of polygons, which can represent lower polyhedra made of triangles and hexagons.  By converting a mesh into a planar graph and then applying the Pach-Angel theorem, we derive an algorithm that transforms N-tetrahedron meshes into diagrams with up to 58 Tets/Hex class polygons, requiring O(N) operations.  Notably, our findings demonstrate that approximately 70% of shapes can be represented using only triangles and hexagons.  Furthermore, we demonstrate the practicality of our approach through proposed applications.

The tasks of relation extraction and knowledge graph link prediction share a
common link in their objectives, allowing them to benefit from each other in the
process of learning. Specifically, KGLP can aid relation extraction by providing
contextual guidance, while RE can help link prediction by enriching textual
representations with relational information. We investigate how RE and KGLP can
be integrated into a unified and iterative framework in which they enhance one
another in a mutually beneficial manner. Experimental results conducted on
public benchmarks confirm that RE and KGLP significantly improve their
respective link prediction and relation linking capabilities when implemented in
a unified and iterative process. Moreover, our analysis reveals the erasability
of the learned knowledge through the application of Jacobian regularization, a
property that enables models to adapt and learn new knowledge in response to
changes during testing.

This study introduces an innovative analytical delay model specifically designed for deep submicron CMOS inverters in the 12nm technology node and beyond, in response to the growing need for advanced modeling techniques in advanced nodes. Developed using Matlab's Curve Fitting Toolbox, the analytical model demonstrates an exceptional fit with simulation-based lookup tables in the 28nm, 20nm, 16nm, 12nm, 14V, 16V, 20V, 24V, 30V, 36V, 40V, 48V, 56V, 64V, 72V, 80V, 88V, 96V, 104V, 112V, 120V, 128V, 136V, 144V, 152V, 160V, 168V, 176V, 184V, 192V, 200V, 210V, 220V, 230V, 240V, 250V, 260V, 270V, 280V, 290V, 300V, 310V,

A widely accepted assumption in both theory and practice is that functions used to model data have a certain level of smoothness. However, most existing approaches use basic distance metrics to measure this, which may not always be suitable for complex, high-dimensional data sets. To address this, we propose a more versatile framework that allows for using custom distance metrics to analyze the smoothness of value functions used in reinforcement learning. This enables more accurate and efficient learning on a variety of real-world tasks, including those set in multi-dimensional space environments and spherical domains. By using custom distance metrics that are better suited to the specific data, our method achieves improved performance over traditional approaches that rely on standard distance metrics.

The ventral temporal cortex in the brain contains intricate patterns of interconnected regions that influence each other in complex ways. A notable pattern exists, where individual faces and human bodies are processed in separate areas, with this phenomenon also observed when tests are conducted in non-human animals. However, it's still unclear to what extent the distinct processing of faces and human bodies in the brain extends to other categories, such as animals. A study using advanced brain imaging technology and mathematical analysis methods examined a vast range of natural images to understand distinct processing within the brain's visual system.
